A.q: How is comprehension defined?

steps.prompt: Comprehension is the goal or purpose for what?
Because comprehension is the goal of reading, it constructs meaning through interaction with what?
Since comprehension uses written language, it is understanding beyond what?
Because comprehension is understanding beyond knowing, it results from what?

A.explain: Comprehension is the goal of reading and simultaneously extracts and constructs meaning from written language. It is understanding beyond knowing, produced by active involvement with text.

A.q: Why is comprehension important?
A.explain: Comprehension leads to better achievement. Without it, readers cannot fully understand content.

A.q: Without comprehension skills, readers cannot do what?
A.explain: Without comprehension skills, readers cannot fully understand content. Active engagement strategies are therefore needed.

A.q: What is the main problem with comprehension?
options: Lacking strategies to engage with text
Reading too many chapters too quickly
Knowing too much prior background information
Using diagrams and printed study materials
A.explain: The main problem is lacking strategies to actively engage with text. Active engagement helps readers understand it.

A.q: Which actions improve comprehension?
options: Be patient with the reading process
Stay with a paragraph until understood
Learn the terminology used in text
Expand your vocabulary regularly over time
Avoid elaborative rehearsal techniques while reading
A.explain: Improving comprehension includes patience, staying with material, learning terminology, and expanding vocabulary. Avoiding rehearsal contradicts active learning.

A.q: Readers should avoid hurrying during what?
A.explain: Be patient means do not rush the reading process. Hurrying can weaken comprehension.

A.q: Readers should stay with a paragraph until what?
A.explain: Stay with a paragraph or section until you comprehend it. This prevents superficial reading.

A.q: Which strategy focuses on specialized words?
A.explain: Learning terminology targets field-specific words. Expanding vocabulary builds general word knowledge.

A.q: Which strategy builds general word knowledge?
A.explain: Expanding vocabulary builds general word knowledge. Terminology focuses on field-specific words.

A.q: Which strategy asks readers to adopt the author's viewpoint?
A.explain: Getting into the writer's head means adopting the author's viewpoint. It supports deeper comprehension.

A.q: When should readers use elaborative rehearsal and active learning?
A.explain: Elaborative rehearsal and active learning techniques are used as you read. They help build comprehension.

A.q: Readers are encouraged to feel what about learning?
A.explain: The strategy is to become excited about what you learn. Positive engagement supports comprehension.

A.q: What does a topic name?
A.explain: The topic is the subject of a paragraph. It can be named in one word or one phrase.

A.q: What does the main idea tell?
A.explain: The main idea tells the point the author intends to develop. It is expressed by the topic sentence when present.

A.q: Match each paragraph element to its role.
A.explain: The topic names the subject, and the main idea states the developed point. The topic sentence acts like an umbrella for supporting details.

A.q: Which statement about a topic sentence is correct?
A.explain: A topic sentence expresses the main idea and usually includes the topic. It is broad enough to include supporting details, but it does not list every detail.

A.q: Why is a topic sentence like an umbrella?
options: It is broad enough to include supporting details
It names only the subject of a paragraph
It appears only as the final paragraph sentence
It develops the whole paragraph for the author
A.explain: The umbrella image means the topic sentence is broad enough to include supporting details. It expresses the main idea and usually includes the topic.

A.q: Match each topic-sentence location to its frequency.
A.explain: Topic sentences most often appear first. They next often appear last, and least often appear in the middle.

A.q: If a main idea is implied, what should a reader do?
A.explain: When a main idea is implied, it is not directly stated in one sentence. The reader should formulate a sentence expressing the overall big picture or main point.

A.q: How many organizational patterns are named?
A.explain: Seven organizational patterns are named. They include chronological, process, comparison or contrast, definition, examples, cause/effect, and whole/parts.

A.q: Which items are organizational patterns?
A.explain: Chronological, process, comparison or contrast, and definition are patterns. A topic sentence expresses a main idea.

A.q: Which additional items are organizational patterns?
A.explain: Examples, cause/effect, and whole/parts complete the seven patterns. Background knowledge is a comprehension-enhancing action.

A.q: What should readers activate to enhance comprehension?
A.explain: Readers activate background knowledge and make associations or connections with text. This engagement supports comprehension.

A.q: Which reader action is called SQ4Rs?
A.explain: SQ4Rs means asking questions before, during, and after reading. Highlighting, reviewing contents, and summarizing once are different actions.

A.q: Awareness of purpose and text features guides what decision?
A.explain: This awareness helps readers decide their reading rate. Purpose and text features affect how fast one should read.

A.q: What comes next in a pre-reading survey?

steps.prompt: After reading the introduction and table of contents, what gives overall topic direction?
After chapter title and subtitles, what indicates what to look for?
After focus questions, what reveals the opening subject?
After first paragraph or introduction, what condenses key takeaway?
After last paragraph or summary, what provides review aids?

A.explain: The survey gives a brief summary before reading. It moves from introduction and contents to titles, focus questions, openings, summaries, and end-of-chapter aids.

A.q: Which statement about focus questions is true?
A.explain: Many, but not all, textbooks include focus questions. Reviewing them shows what to look for.

A.q: What should readers do during reading review?
A.explain: Reading review means taking notes or highlighting important concepts. It happens while engaging with the text.

A.q: What does post-reading review identify?
A.explain: Post-reading review identifies learned concepts and important takeaways. It also reveals concepts that are not fully comprehended.

A.q: Why identify unclear concepts after reading?
options: To spend more time reviewing them
To skip the chapter summary now
To avoid active engagement during reading
To reduce vocabulary learning over time
A.explain: Identifying unclear concepts lets readers spend more time reviewing them. This strengthens comprehension.
